items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? Give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies water as the solvent in an aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Defines an aqueous solution as a solution in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is the solvent or that the solute is dissolved in water.

rubric.why: Gives a valid example of a solute dissolved in water.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as sodium chloride or sugar dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
Example: sodium chloride dissolved in water (salt water).

items.followUp: Define molar concentration and state its unit.

rubric.why: Defines concentration in terms of the amount of solute in a specified volume of solution.
rubric.description: Defines concentration as the amount of solute dissolved in a unit volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition using amount of solute and unit volume of solution.

rubric.why: States a valid unit used for concentration.
rubric.description: Names a unit of concentration, such as mol dm⁻³ or g dm⁻³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct unit, stated by name or notation.

modelAnswer: Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a unit volume of solution.
A common unit is mole per cubic decimetre (mol dm⁻³).

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of lithium greater than that of sodium?

rubric.why: Explains that sodium’s outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded than potassium’s.
rubric.description: Sodium has a smaller atomic radius and fewer occupied electron shells than potassium, so its outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of atomic size, distance from the nucleus, number of shells, or shielding.

rubric.why: Connects the stronger attraction in sodium to the greater energy required to remove its outer electron.
rubric.description: Sodium’s outer electron is held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it than in potassium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the stronger attraction or that more energy is required to remove the electron.

modelAnswer: Sodium has a smaller atomic radius and fewer occupied electron shells than potassium, so its outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
The nucleus attracts sodium’s outer electron more strongly; therefore, more energy is needed to remove it.

items.followUp: Write any five characteristics of a compound.

rubric.why: Identifies that the proportions of components in a mixture can vary.
rubric.description: A mixture has variable composition; its components may be present in any proportion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the composition or proportions are not fixed.

rubric.why: Recognizes that the components retain their individual properties in a mixture.
rubric.description: The components retain their individual properties.

rubric.why: Identifies that mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: The components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating physical separability or giving a valid physical separation method.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a mixture from substances formed by chemical combination.
rubric.description: The components are not chemically combined with one another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the components are not chemically combined.

rubric.why: Identifies a further characteristic of mixtures: they lack a definite formula or fixed characteristic melting or boiling point.
rubric.description: A mixture has no definite chemical formula or fixed melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid characteristic not already counted.

modelAnswer: A mixture has a variable composition; its components may be present in any proportion.
The components retain their individual properties.
The components can be separated by physical methods.
The components are not chemically combined.
A mixture has no definite chemical formula or fixed melting or boiling point.
